title: Psycho-physiological restoration with audio-visual interactions through virtual reality simulations of soundscape and landscape experiences in urban, waterfront, and green environments
research_question: To comprehensively investigate the effect of soundscape and landscape experiences on psycho-physiological restoration responses from the viewpoint of audio-visual interactions and to propose a restoration model that could be directly applied to space design.

participants.description: 60 university/graduate students (30 male, 30 female) aged 21-30 years (mean 24.3, SD 2.4) living in Seoul, Korea, with typical vision and hearing, and physically healthy with mild depression, stress, or anxiety.
participants.recruitment: Announcements posted on message boards and social network services of universities in Seoul.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Virtual reality simulations of 9 real-world urban, waterfront, and green environments in Korea. Each simulation included panoramic 360° visual data (8k resolution) and 4-channel ambisonic audio data, synchronized and presented via HMD (VIVE Pro Eye, HTC) and open-type headphones (HD-650, Sennheiser). Stimuli lasted 3 minutes each.

measures.instrument: 14 semantic expressions (pleasant, vibrant, eventful, informative, annoying, stressful, chaotic, artificial, uninformative, calm, relaxing, natural, monotonous, uneventful) on a 5-point Likert scale, factor-analyzed into Supportive, Detrimental, Tranquil soundscape.
3-item Likert scale (1-5) for overall impression, appropriateness, sound satisfaction.

14 semantic attributes (appealing, harmonious, orderly, repulsive, disharmonious, disorderly, complex, simple, open, natural, wide, enclosed, artificial, narrow) on a 5-point Likert scale, factor-analyzed into Attractive, Discomforting, Spatial/Natural landscape.
3-item Likert scale (1-5) for scenic beauty, status of infrastructure, visual satisfaction.
19-item scale (1-7) across 6 domains: Fascination, Being away to, Being away from, Compatibility, Extent (Coherence), Extent (Scope).
Positive Affect and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) (1-5 scale)
SA-3000NEW (Medicore) measuring Total Power (TP), Standard Deviation of Normal to Normal (SDNN), Temporary Stationarity Index (TSI), Low Frequency (LF), Heart Rate (HR).
32-channel EPOC Flex (EMOTIV) EEG measuring alpha/beta ratio (ABR).
140-item scale (1-5) for Novelty Seeking, Harm Avoidance, Reward Dependence, Persistence, Self-Directedness, Cooperativeness, Self-Transcendence.
WHOQOL-BREF (26-item scale, 1-5) across 4 domains: Physical, Psychological, Social, Environmental.
Urban Residents Psychological Security (URPS) (20-item scale, 1-5) across 4 domains: Self-psychological, Social, Social environmental risk perception, Natural environmental security.

mechanisms: Natural environments facilitate involuntary attention (fascination) and provide a sense of escaping from daily responsibilities, leading to psychological restoration.
Natural environments offer greater compatibility, consistency, and richness, reducing the need for focused attention and promoting psychological restoration.
Natural environments induce calmer emotional states (higher valence, lower arousal) and reduce negative affect, contributing to stress recovery.
Waterfront environments specifically increase autonomic nervous system activity (TP, SDNN) and reduce physiological stress (TSI), indicating physiological restoration.
Urban environments, despite being less restorative overall, can still induce some physiological restoration (e.g., increased SDNN) due to participants' familiarity and adaptation to urban stimuli.
The 'sense of liberation' (being away to/from) from an environment is linked to physiological recovery and sympathetic nervous system vitalization.

Audio-visual interactions: Artificial sound/visual elements (traffic, buildings, human sound, music, grey ratio, loudness, LAeq, LA5-A95) negatively impact perceived environmental quality and psychological restoration. Natural sound/visual elements (birdsongs, water, wind, vegetation, open space, sky, green ratio, water ratio) positively impact these outcomes.

Perceived affective qualities (tranquil soundscape, attractive/spatial/natural landscape) are positively associated with psychological restoration, while detrimental soundscape and discomforting landscape are negatively associated.
Overall environmental quality (impression, appropriateness, sound/visual satisfaction, scenic beauty) is strongly associated with psychological restoration.
moderators: Individual characteristics (e.g., personality traits, temperament, health state, noise sensitivity) were examined but showed low explanatory power (under 2%) for psycho-physiological responses.
implementation_implications: Urban space planning should aim to decrease detrimental soundscapes and discomforting landscapes by controlling artificial elements (e.g., traffic, buildings, noise) both visually and acoustically.

Urban space planning should aim to increase supportive or tranquil soundscapes and attractive, spatial, or natural landscapes by increasing natural elements (e.g., parks, water fountains, man-made rivers, vegetation, water, sky, birdsong).
Designers should prioritize creating visually attractive and spatial-natural landscapes and acoustically supportive and tranquil soundscapes to improve restoration response.
Controlling physical noise levels (LAeq, LA5-A95, Loudness) alone is insufficient; a soundscape perspective using sound as a valuable resource is needed.
Providing natural elements can mask unavoidable urban noises and offer restorative effects.
Managing human crowd density is important, as excessive density negatively impacts restoration; appropriate density can promote comfort and positive activities.
The proposed models can help urban designers, planners, and decision-makers prioritize physical characteristics for promoting urbanites' health improvement.
The models can serve as basic data for developing healthy environments and urban improvement plans.

limitations: Study conducted with participants aged 20-29 years, limiting generalizability to other age groups.
Findings did not reflect sociocultural differences, as all participants were Korean and lived in a city.
Investigated short-term responses, necessitating investigation of long-term restorative effects of continuous exposure.
Used HMD headphone-based VR technology, which might not be as immersive as augmented reality or mixed reality, potentially affecting ecological validity.
Only analyzed mean brain wave values; future research should explore alpha and beta waves in different brain regions or functional connectivity.
Did not assess other physiological responses (e.g., blood, hormones, brain images) beyond HRV and EEG.
